title: The Other Energy Shock

The Other Energy Shock

Wei He

Gavekal Dragonomics | 9 Oct 2026

With global oil prices still over US$100 a barrel as the Iran conflict drags on, China’s government is proudly trumpeting how its distinctive energy strategy has allowed it to weather the impact. Thanks to abundant domestic coal supplies and rapid development of renewables, oil accounts for just 18% of China’s total energy consumption. Coal is still over half, and as a result government officials claim China has been able to escape the damage from shortages seen in other countries. “Coal is our greatest source of confidence in maintaining stable energy supplies,” declared Wang Hongzhi, the head of the National Energy Administration, in June.This rhetoric obscures the fact that in recent months China has been experiencing a coal-supply shock, and that this shock is entirely domestic in origin. After a major mining accident in Shanxi province, a sweeping safety drive has depressed coal output and pushed up prices. The central role of coal in stabilizing the energy system makes it all the more surprising that China’s policymakers chose to restrict its supply at this juncture. The episode underscores how government officials, far from seeking economic stability at all costs, are willing to tolerate somewhat higher energy prices and slower growth as they prioritize other policy aims and focus on the domestic political cycle (see Governance Over Growth).
